pages.x: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast of Mexico with about 500 men, 16 horses and a few cannon, against the orders of the governor of Cuba. So that no one could turn back, he had his ships run aground and sunk.

A Nahua woman given to the Spaniards as a slave, Malintzin, called La Malinche, spoke both Maya and Nahuatl, and soon Spanish. She became Cortés's voice and adviser. To some Mexicans her name has stood for betrayal; to others, for survival.

Many peoples hated paying tribute to the Mexica. The Tlaxcalans, their old enemies, joined the Spaniards with thousands of warriors, and others followed. Without them the conquest could never have happened.

Moctezuma II welcomed the strangers into Tenochtitlan in November 1519. Within days Cortés made him a prisoner in his own palace. In June 1520 Moctezuma died, stoned by his own people, the Spaniards said, and they fled the city by night, losing hundreds of men.

Then smallpox arrived with a later Spanish expedition. The peoples of Mexico had never met it, and it killed perhaps half of Tenochtitlan, among them the new emperor, Cuitláhuac. In 1521 Cortés came back with his allies and took the city after a long siege.
The last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, led the defence to the end and was captured in August 1521. He was later tortured for gold and hanged in 1525. Mexico honours him as the hero who would not give in.

In 1532 Francisco Pizarro, with 168 men, met the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, just after he had won a civil war against his brother. In a surprise attack the Spaniards killed thousands of his followers and seized him. Atahualpa offered to fill a room once with gold and twice with silver for his freedom.

The ransom was paid and melted into bars, and Pizarro had Atahualpa executed anyway in 1533. The Spaniards took Cusco, the Inca capital. Inca resistance went on in the mountains until 1572, when the last emperor, Túpac Amaru, was beheaded.

Within a century most of the native peoples of Mexico and Peru were dead, nine in ten by many estimates. Most died of new diseases, smallpox, measles and typhus, made worse by war, forced labour and hunger.

pages.x: The conquests gave Spain an empire and a flood of silver that changed the world's economy, and made Spanish the language of most of the Americas. They also began a new, mixed people and culture, and Mexico today honours both its Aztec and its Spanish past.
pts: Disease killed most of the native peoples
